reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes paid OneCoin packages costing EUR 100 to EUR 5,000 as a route to mining profits, including an example of EUR 300 in immediate returns from a EUR 3,000 package. It links financial rewards to inviting successive partners and uses projected five- to tenfold coin appreciation to support the opportunity, although the speaker denies that the company is a pyramid and the records do not establish that any payment, mining, exchange listing, or reward was completed.

opening.argument: The presentation does not promise that projected coin prices will materialize: the speaker explicitly says there are no guarantees and ties outcomes to supply and demand. Mining, exchange access, and future purchases are described as planned stages, not completed events. That makes the claims conditional forecasts about a proposed market, rather than proof that viewers were assured a return. The speaker also acknowledges that the cryptocurrency market includes fake and scam activity, showing that the presentation does not treat every crypto offer as trustworthy.

citations.quote: but there are no guarantees here, everything depends exclusively on the ratio of supply-purchase the demand for proposals
I plan to do it within 2016
there is many fake and scam on the market, which involves the crypto currency

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution points to packages, mining rights, recruitment commissions, and appreciation projections, but those facts do not establish that a return was guaranteed or that mining or rewards occurred. The speaker qualifies the price forecast as having no guarantees and describes mining and exchange functions as future plans. A commercial presentation of a risky proposal is not, on this evidence alone, proof of deception.

citations.quote: but there are no guarantees here, everything depends exclusively on the ratio of supply-purchase the demand for proposals
I plan to do it within 2016

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A no-guarantee disclaimer does not change what is being promoted: paid packages include tokens described as rights to mine for profit, and the presentation forecasts substantial appreciation. Future-oriented wording may mean the promised operation had not begun, but it does not make the solicitation a neutral market forecast. Acknowledging that scams exist in cryptocurrency does not establish that this particular offer is safe.

opening.argument: This is structured as an explanatory presentation: it walks through cryptocurrency, mining, blockchain, tokens, and the stages the company says it plans to develop. The speaker explains mining with an algorithm analogy and shows a blockchain example, while describing an academy with courses and quizzes. Those are educational and technical subjects; the presence of a commercial opportunity does not by itself show that the video’s central function is to document completed fraud or guarantee an investment outcome.

citations.quote: Cryptocurrency is a mathematical algorithm
these are videos courses are and these are quizzes at the end of each level of training
Blockchain. This is basically a straight transmission.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution’s examples show what the presentation explains, not that those claims were independently verified or that viewers received the described returns. A token is defined, mining is illustrated, and a commission example is discussed; none proves that mining, exchange listing, or payment actually occurred. The material’s future-tense language is important when distinguishing an explanation of a proposed system from evidence of a completed scam.

citations.quote: A token is a right to mine one coin to make a profit.
our one-coin mining begins
somewhere in April we can sell already coins

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The educational format is embedded in a sales pitch, not separated from it: the video presents paid packages as a route to tokens and mining, then explains how partner recruitment produces commissions. Teaching terminology does not neutralize those solicitations. The speaker’s own definition connects a token to mining for profit, while the package slide supplies prices.

citations.quote: A token is a right to mine one coin to make a profit.
when these partners start to invite the following partners

opening.argument: The video presents a package-based business and educational service, with tiered prices and associated course levels, tokens, and account features. That is evidence of a commercial offer, but the record does not show a viewer paying, credentials being requested, or any promised mining or reward being delivered. Nor does a displayed commission calculation establish that a participant actually earned that amount. Without those observed outcomes, the presentation supports a description of the offer, not a finding that its mechanism operated as represented.

citations.quote: Plus, together with the learning package there are also tokens.
our one-coin mining begins

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats package prices, mining language, and recruitment commissions as if they establish completed payments and payouts. They do not: the cited commission passage describes what would accumulate as partners invite others, while mining and coin sales are discussed as forthcoming. The presentation contains a commercial proposal, but the supplied material does not show a completed transaction or realized return.

citations.quote: when these partners start to invite the following partners
our one-coin mining begins
somewhere in April we can sell already coins

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing proof of completed payouts is not a defense to the content of the promotion. The packages are expressly linked to tokens, the speaker calls a token a right to mine for profit, and the presentation describes commissions generated through successive partner invitations. Those are the proposed earning mechanisms, even if this video alone does not establish that anyone ultimately received the money.
